title: Pinch pot crescent moon candle holder
subtitle: A hollow crescent moon form built from two joined pinch pots, sized to hold a tea light
excerpt: A crescent moon candle holder is two pinch pots joined at their rims to form a hollow body, then trimmed into a crescent arc. This version uses air-dry clay with no kiln. The finished piece holds a standard 38 mm tea light inside the hollow centre.
sourceNotes: Technique derived from first principles. V&A open-access collection for decorative ceramic form reference.

glossaryTerms.definition: A hand-building technique where a ball of clay is opened and thinned by pressing the thumb inside while rotating and pinching the walls
The joining method: roughen both surfaces with a needle tool, apply clay slip, then press together firmly
The drying stage where clay holds its shape firmly but is still damp enough to carve, trim, and join
Fully air-dried and unfired; pale, lightweight, and fragile, ready for sealing

content.text: A crescent moon candle holder is a hollow air-dry clay form that holds a tea light inside its body, no kiln required. Two
pinch pots

are joined rim to rim to create a sealed sphere, then trimmed into a crescent arc at the leather-hard stage. The finished holder is 14 cm at the widest point and fits a standard 38 mm tea light in the opening cut at the top.

materials.name: Clay slip (same clay body, thinned with water to double-cream consistency)
Acrylic paint (optional, for decorating after sealing)

tools.name: Fettling knife (for trimming the crescent arc)

content.text: Preparation

Air-dry clay sets at room temperature without a kiln: work at a steady pace to prevent the outer surface drying while the walls are still soft. Keep a small bowl of water nearby and cover unused clay with a damp cloth or sealed bag. Work on a piece of canvas, a cloth-covered board, or a sheet of baking parchment so the base does not stick to your work surface. Make your clay slip before starting: pinch a small piece of clay into a cup of water and stir until the mixture is the consistency of double cream.
Making the two pinch pots
Divide the clay into two equal balls of around 120 g each. Roll each into a smooth sphere between your palms.
Hold one ball in your non-dominant hand. Press your dominant thumb into the centre to a depth of about 2 cm, stopping at least 1 cm from the base.
Rotate the ball slowly in your palm while pinching the wall between thumb and forefinger, working the clay upward and outward. Aim for a wall thickness of 5-6 mm throughout.
Open the rim of the pot until the diameter reaches 8-9 cm. Smooth the rim flat with a damp finger so both pots will sit flush when joined.

Repeat with the second ball to make an identical pot. Place both face-down on your board and allow them to stiffen for 20 minutes. They need to hold their dome shape when placed rim-to-rim without collapsing.
Joining the pots
Use the needle tool to
score and slip
both rims. Scratch a cross-hatch pattern 2-3 mm deep across the full width of each rim, then apply a generous coat of clay slip.
Press the two rims together firmly. Rock the joined sphere gently to close any gaps. Hold for 30 seconds while the slip begins to grip.
Blend the exterior seam with a dampened finger, smoothing from the join line outward. Use a wooden rib to compress the seam further, working around the full circumference.

Poke a small air hole in the top of the sphere with the needle tool. This prevents the trapped air expanding as the clay dries and cracking the walls. The hole will be hidden when you cut the tea-light opening later.
Shaping the crescent
Allow the joined sphere to firm to
leather-hard
stage: roughly 1-2 hours at room temperature. The surface should feel cool and firm but not dry or pale.

Draw your crescent arc on the sphere with the needle tool. The crescent runs from a point at the top through a wide arc to a point at the bottom. The outer edge of the arc follows the widest curve of the sphere; the inner edge cuts across a chord roughly 4 cm inside the outer edge.

Use a fettling knife or needle tool to carefully cut away the clay outside your inner crescent line. Work in thin passes, removing 2-3 mm at a time rather than cutting through in one stroke. The crescent shape now has a hollow interior visible from the side.
Cut a circular opening 40 mm across in the top face of the crescent body. This is where the tea light sits. Smooth the cut edge with a damp finger.
If you want star or dot pierced decorations on the crescent body, press through now with the needle tool. Keep holes at least 6 mm from any edge to avoid cracking.

Smooth all cut edges and the exterior with a lightly dampened pottery sponge. Stand the crescent with its flat cut face forward and check it sits stable. Press a small clay coil to the very base as a foot if the piece rocks.
Drying
Allow the crescent to dry completely at room temperature before sealing. The piece goes through three stages: soft clay when freshly shaped, then
leather-hard
when firm and cool to the touch, then
bone-dry

when pale and no longer cold. Bone-dry typically takes two to three days. Do not try to speed drying with heat: forced drying causes cracking, especially through the joined seam. Turn the piece once during drying so air reaches all surfaces.
Finishing

Once bone-dry, apply two coats of 50/50 PVA and water to all exterior surfaces. Allow each coat to dry fully before adding the next. PVA sealer hardens the surface and reduces the risk of the clay softening in humid conditions. Paint with acrylic colours before the final PVA coat if you want a coloured finish: a deep indigo with silver star highlights suits the moon theme.
Care and safety

This holder is decorative only. Use only genuine tea lights in a metal cup, not loose wax. Do not leave burning candles unattended. The interior of the hollow body will warm but the air-dry clay walls will not catch fire from the tea-light flame alone. Keep away from flammable materials. Wipe the exterior with a dry cloth only: prolonged moisture contact will soften sealed air-dry clay over time.
Variations

Scale the sphere up to 180 g per half-pot for a candle holder that fits a pillar candle in a glass holder rather than a bare tea light. The opening needs to match your glass diameter exactly, so measure the glass before cutting.

Press a face into the crescent at the leather-hard stage: two almond-shaped eye depressions and a small curved nose suggest a stylised moon face. Keep the features shallow so they read clearly after painting.
Make three holders in graduating sizes from 80 g, 120 g, and 200 g balls, and group them on a small tray to create a moon phase display.

items.problem: Seam cracked where the two pots were joined
items.cause: The rims were not scored and slipped thoroughly, or the clay was too dry at the join point
items.fix: At leather-hard, dampen the crack line, score both sides of the crack, apply fresh slip, and press closed. Support the seam with a thin clay coil on the interior if you can reach it

items.problem: Sphere collapsed when the crescent was cut
items.cause: The clay was too soft when cutting; the hollow walls could not support the open form
items.fix: Allow the joined sphere to reach a firm leather-hard state before cutting. If already collapsed, press the walls back to shape from inside with a damp finger and allow to re-firm before continuing

items.problem: Air hole caused a visible crack in the top of the sphere
items.cause: The hole was made too close to the seam line, or the hole was too large
items.fix: Keep air holes to 3 mm diameter and place them away from the join seam. Small surface cracks at leather-hard can be filled with a paste of clay and water, then smoothed over

items.problem: Tea light does not sit level in the opening
items.cause: The cut opening is not perfectly circular or the crescent does not stand with the opening facing upward
items.fix: Check the base stability first. Add a small clay foot coil to level the piece. Enlarge the opening slightly with a needle tool to accommodate the tea-light cup
